questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, One Assertion [A ] and the other Reason [ R ] are given. Identify the correct option Assertion [A]: The decreasing order of the acidic character of the following is $\mathrm{B} \gt \mathrm{D} \gt \mathrm{A} \gt \mathrm{C}$
Reason $[\mathrm{R}]$ : Fluorine has larger -I effect than Cl and Br .
options: A is wrong but R is correct.
Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A .
Both $A$ and $R$ are correct and $R$ is the correct explanation of $A$.
questions.solution:
The acidity of substituted cyclohexanols is determined by the inductive effect (-I effect) of the substituent. The -I effect increases the acidity of the hydroxyl group by stabilizing the conjugate base (alkoxide ion) through electron withdrawal.

The strength of the -I effect follows the order: F > Cl > Br. The methyl group (-C$H_{3}$) exhibits a +I effect, which destabilizes the conjugate base and decreases acidity compared to the unsubstituted cyclohexanol. \\ \\ Comparing the structures: \\ [A] 4-bromocyclohexanol: -I effect of Br. \\ [B] 2-chlorocyclohexanol: -I effect of Cl at the ortho position. \\ [C] 2-methylcyclohexanol: +I effect of CH_{3}$ at the ortho position.
[D] 4-fluorocyclohexanol: -I effect of F.

The -I effect is distance-dependent. Substituents at the 2-position (ortho) have a stronger effect than those at the 4-position (para). Thus, the order of acidity is determined by the strength of the -I effect and the proximity to the -OH group. The order is [B] (Cl at 2-position) > [D] (F at 4-position) > [A] (Br at 4-position) > [C] (CH_{3}$ at 2-position).

Assertion [A] states the order B > D > A > C, which is correct. Reason [R] states that Fluorine has a larger -I effect than Cl and Br, which is also correct. However, the reason for the order B > D is the proximity of the substituent (ortho vs para), not just the strength of the -I effect of the halogen itself. Therefore, R is not the correct explanation for A.

Answer: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A .

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Arrange the following in the decreasing order of their $\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{a}}$ values.
questions.solution:
The acidity of phenols is determined by the stability of the phenoxide ion formed after the loss of a proton. Electron-withdrawing groups (EWG) increase acidity (lower $\text{pK}_{\text{a}}$), while electron-donating groups (EDG) decrease acidity (higher $\text{pK}_{\text{a}}$).

The substituents at the para position for the given compounds are:
[A] $-\text{NH}_{2}$: Strong electron-donating group by resonance ($+M$).
[B] $-\text{NO}_{2}$: Strong electron-withdrawing group by resonance ($-M$) and induction ($-I$).
[C] $-\text{OCH}_{3}$: Electron-donating group by resonance ($+M$) but electron-withdrawing by induction ($-I$). Overall, it acts as a weak electron donor.
[D] $-\text{Cl}$: Electron-withdrawing group by induction ($-I$) but electron-donating by resonance ($+M$). Overall, it acts as a weak electron withdrawer.

Comparing the electron-donating/withdrawing effects:
The $-\text{NH}_{2}$ group is the strongest electron donor, making [A] the least acidic (highest $\text{pK}_{\text{a}}$).
The $-\text{OCH}_{3}$ group is a weaker electron donor than $-\text{NH}_{2}$, making [C] less acidic than [D] and [B] but more acidic than [A].
The $-\text{Cl}$ group is an electron withdrawer, making [D] more acidic than [A] and [C].
The $-\text{NO}_{2}$ group is the strongest electron withdrawer, making [B] the most acidic (lowest $\text{pK}_{\text{a}}$).

The acidity order is $\text{B} \gt \text{D} \gt \text{C} \gt \text{A}$.
Since $\text{pK}_{\text{a}}$ is inversely proportional to acidity, the decreasing order of $\text{pK}_{\text{a}}$ values is $\text{A} \gt \text{C} \gt \text{D} \gt \text{B}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{A} \gt \mathrm{C} \gt \mathrm{D} \gt \mathrm{B}$

Cyclohexanol undergoes a series of reactions as given. Identify compound (iv).
$\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_{11} \mathrm{OH}+\mathrm{CrO}_3 \rightarrow(\mathrm{i})+\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5 \mathrm{MgI} \rightarrow(\mathrm{ii})+\text { dil. } \mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow(\mathrm{iii})+\text { Conc. } \mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4 \rightarrow(\mathrm{iv})$
questions.solution:
$C_6H_{11}OH + CrO_3 \rightarrow$ Cyclohexanone (i) — $CrO_3$ oxidises secondary alcohol to ketone.

3: Cyclohexanone $+ C_6H_5MgI \rightarrow$ then dil. $HCl$ — Grignard reagent adds phenyl group to carbonyl carbon, followed by protonation to give 1-phenylcyclohexanol (iii) — a tertiary alcohol.

1-phenylcyclohexanol $+$ Conc. $H_3PO_4 \rightarrow$ dehydration (E1), loss of $H_2O$ gives 1-phenylcyclohexene (iv) — double bond forms in conjugation with phenyl ring for maximum stability.

Compound (iv) is 1-phenylcyclohexene — option (4).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Benzene diazonium chloride when warmed with water gives a compound, whose Sodium salt when reacted with Allyl bromide gives compound $[\mathrm{X}]$. Identify $[\mathrm{X}]$.
questions.solution:
Benzene diazonium chloride warmed with water \rightarrow Phenol ($C_6H_5OH$) + $N_2\uparrow$ + $HCl$

Phenol + NaOH \rightarrow Sodium phenoxide ($C_6H_5O^-Na^+$)

Williamson ether synthesis — sodium phenoxide reacts with allyl bromide ($CH_2=CH-CH_2Br$) via $S_N2$:

$C_6H_5O^-Na^+ + Br-CH_2-CH=CH_2 \rightarrow C_6H_5-O-CH_2-CH=CH_2 + NaBr$

X is allyl phenyl ether: $C_6H_5-O-CH_2-CH=CH_2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Identify [ X ], the final product formed when 2 moles of Ethanal undergoes the following series of reactions with reagents [(i) to (iv)]
$\underset{2 \text { moles }}{\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CHO}} \xrightarrow[\text { (iii). } \mathrm{NaBH}_4 \text { (iv). } \dfrac{C r_2 O_7^{2-}}{H^{+}}]{\text {(i). dil } \mathrm{NaOH} \text { (ii) Heat. }}[\mathrm{X}]$
questions.solution:
The reaction of 2 moles of ethanal with dil. $\mathrm{NaOH}$ is an aldol condensation reaction. The two molecules of $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO}$ undergo condensation to form 3-hydroxybutanal: $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO} + \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CHO} \xrightarrow{\text{dil. NaOH}} \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH(OH)CH}_2\mathrm{CHO}$.

Heating 3-hydroxybutanal leads to dehydration via the E1cB mechanism, resulting in the formation of an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated aldehyde, which is but-2-enal (crotonaldehyde): $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH(OH)CH}_2\mathrm{CHO} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH=CHCHO} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$.

The reagent $\mathrm{NaBH}_4$ is a selective reducing agent that reduces the aldehyde group to a primary alcohol while leaving the carbon-carbon double bond intact: $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH=CHCHO} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaBH}_4} \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH=CHCH}_2\mathrm{OH}$ (but-2-en-1-ol).

Finally, the oxidation of the primary alcohol using $\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}/\mathrm{H}^{+}$ (Jones oxidation or similar strong oxidizing conditions) converts the primary alcohol group to a carboxylic acid group, yielding but-2-enoic acid: $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH=CHCH}_2\mathrm{OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}/\mathrm{H}^{+}} \mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH=CHCOOH}$.

Answer: But-2-enoic acid

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An organic compound $[\mathrm{X}]$ reacts with $\mathrm{H}_2 / \mathrm{Pd}-\mathrm{BaSO}_4$ to give compound $[\mathrm{Y}]$ which reduces Tollen's reagent and undergoes Cannizzaro's reaction. On rigorous oxidation of [Y] in presence of $\mathrm{KMnO}_4 / \mathrm{H}^{+}$Phthalic acid is the product obtained. What is $[\mathrm{X}]$ ?
questions.solution:
The reaction of an organic compound [X] with $H_{2}/Pd-BaSO_{4}$ (Rosenmund reduction) indicates that [X] is an acid chloride ($R-COCl$).

The product [Y] obtained from this reduction is an aldehyde ($R-CHO$).

Since [Y] reduces Tollen's reagent and undergoes Cannizzaro's reaction, [Y] must be an aromatic aldehyde (as it lacks $\alpha$-hydrogens).

Rigorous oxidation of [Y] with $KMnO_{4}/H^{+}$ yields phthalic acid. Phthalic acid is benzene-1,2-dicarboxylic acid. This implies that the starting material [X] must be an ortho-substituted benzene derivative with a $-COCl$ group and another group that can be oxidized to a $-COOH$ group at the ortho position.

The structure of phthalic acid is a benzene ring with two $-COOH$ groups at the 1 and 2 positions. Therefore, the precursor [Y] must be 2-methylbenzaldehyde (o-tolualdehyde), which upon oxidation gives phthalic acid. Consequently, the compound [X] must be 2-methylbenzoyl chloride.

Comparing this with the given options, the structure corresponding to 2-methylbenzoyl chloride is the one with a $-COCl$ group and a $-CH_{3}$ group at the ortho position.

Answer:

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two statements, one Assertion (A) and the other Reason (R) are given. Choose the correct option. Assertion: Compound $[\mathrm{X}]$ reacts with Hydrazine in presence of $\mathrm{KOH} /$ Glycol to form the product $[\mathrm{Y}]$.
options: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A .
Both $A$ and $R$ are correct but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$.
A is wrong but R is correct.
questions.solution:
The reaction shown is the Wolff-Kishner reduction, which uses hydrazine ($NH_{2}NH_{2}$) in the presence of a strong base like $KOH$ and a high-boiling solvent like ethylene glycol to reduce a carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone) to a methylene group ($-CH_{2}-$).

In the given reaction, the aldehyde group ($-CHO$) in compound [X] is reduced to a methyl group ($-CH_{3}$) to form compound [Y].

The Wolff-Kishner reduction is specifically designed to reduce carbonyl compounds to alkanes. It does not affect other functional groups like alkyl halides under standard conditions, although strong bases like $KOH$ can potentially cause elimination reactions in alkyl halides. However, in the context of this transformation, the conversion of the aldehyde to the methyl group is the primary intended reaction.

Since the assertion correctly describes the transformation of [X] to [Y] using the Wolff-Kishner reduction conditions, and the reaction is indeed a standard application of this named reaction, the assertion is correct.

Answer: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A .

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which one of the following reactions does not give the correct combination of reactants and the major products formed in the reaction?
questions.solution:
Option (8BNT6): Acetaldehyde reacts with ethanol in the presence of dry HCl gas to form an acetal, $\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{CH}(\mathrm{OC}_2\mathrm{H}_5)_2$. This is a correct reaction.

Option (kuGqc): Acetophenone contains a methyl ketone group, which undergoes the iodoform reaction with $\mathrm{I}_2$ and $\mathrm{Na}_2\mathrm{CO}_3$ to produce $\mathrm{CHI}_3$ and the benzoate salt $\mathrm{C}_6\mathrm{H}_5\mathrm{COO}^-$. This is a correct reaction.

Option (ZY1se): Acetone reacts with semicarbazide in a weakly basic medium to form the corresponding semicarbazone, $(\mathrm{CH}_3)_2\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{N}-\mathrm{NH}-\mathrm{CO}-\mathrm{NH}_2$. This is a correct reaction.

Option (EtplL): DIBAL-H is a selective reducing agent that reduces nitriles to aldehydes. However, DIBAL-H does not reduce carbon-carbon double bonds. The reaction of $\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CN}$ with DIBAL-H followed by hydrolysis should yield $\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CHO}$, not the saturated aldehyde $\mathrm{CH}_3-(\mathrm{CH}_2)_4-\mathrm{CHO}$. Thus, this reaction is incorrect.

Answer: $\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CN} \xrightarrow[\text { (ii). } \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}]{\text { (i). DIBAL - } \mathrm{H}} \mathrm{CH}_3-\left(\mathrm{CH}_2\right)_4-\mathrm{CHO}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
An organic compound $[\mathrm{X}]$ (molecular formula- $\mathrm{C}_5 \mathrm{H}_{11} \mathrm{NO}$ when reacted with $\mathrm{Br}_2 /$ aq. NaOH yielded [Y] which reacts with $\mathrm{CHCl}_3$ and Ethanolic KOH to produce a foul smelling compound.
Compound $[\mathrm{Y}]$ also reacts with HONO to produce Butan-1-ol with liberation of $\mathrm{N}_2(\mathrm{~g})$. Identify [X].
questions.solution:
The reaction of compound [X] with $\mathrm{Br}_2 / \mathrm{aq. NaOH}$ is the Hofmann bromamide degradation reaction, which converts an amide ($\mathrm{R-CONH}_2$) into a primary amine ($\mathrm{R-NH}_2$).

The product [Y] reacts with $\mathrm{CHCl}_3$ and ethanolic $\mathrm{KOH}$ to produce a foul-smelling compound (isocyanide test), confirming that [Y] is a primary aliphatic amine.

The reaction of [Y] with $\mathrm{HONO}$ (nitrous acid) produces Butan-1-ol with the liberation of $\mathrm{N}_2$ gas. This indicates that the amine [Y] is Butan-1-amine, $\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{NH}_2$.

Since the Hofmann bromamide degradation results in the loss of the carbonyl carbon atom, the original amide [X] must have one more carbon atom than the amine [Y]. Thus, [X] is a pentanamide with the formula $\mathrm{C}_5\mathrm{H}_{11}\mathrm{NO}$.

The structure of the amide corresponding to Butan-1-amine is $\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CONH}_2$.

Answer: $\mathrm{CH}_3-\left(\mathrm{CH}_2\right)_3-\mathrm{CONH}_2$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, one Assertion (A) and the other Reason (R) are given. Choose the correct option.
Assertion: 2-aminoethanoic acid and p-aminobenzene sulphonic acid can exist as Zwitter ions while p-aminobenzoic acid cannot.
Reason: When the acid group is a relatively strong proton donor and the $-\mathrm{NH}_2$ group is sufficiently basic it can accept a $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ion from the acid group to form the dipolar ion.
options: Both A and R are correct but R is not the correct explanation of A .
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A .
A is wrong but R is correct.
questions.solution:
A Zwitter ion is formed when an acidic group (proton donor) and a basic group (proton acceptor) are present in the same molecule, allowing for internal proton transfer. 2-aminoethanoic acid (glycine) contains a carboxylic acid group ($-COOH$) and an amino group ($-NH_2$), which allows it to exist as $H_3N^{+}-CH_2-COO^{-}$.

p-aminobenzene sulphonic acid (sulphanilic acid) contains a strongly acidic sulphonic acid group ($-SO_3H$) and a basic amino group ($-NH_2$), which allows it to exist as a Zwitter ion $H_3N^{+}-C_6H_4-SO_3^{-}$.

p-aminobenzoic acid contains a carboxylic acid group ($-COOH$) and an amino group ($-NH_2$). However, the basicity of the amino group attached to the benzene ring is significantly reduced due to resonance with the aromatic ring. Consequently, it is not basic enough to accept a proton from the carboxylic acid group to form a stable Zwitter ion in aqueous solution.

The Reason (R) correctly explains the requirement for Zwitter ion formation: the acid group must be a strong enough proton donor and the amino group must be sufficiently basic to accept the proton. Since the Assertion (A) correctly identifies the compounds that can form Zwitter ions and the Reason (R) provides the correct chemical principle, both are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.

Answer: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A .

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, one Assertion (A) and the other Reason (R) are given. Choose the correct option.
Assertion: Maltose, a disaccharide, is a reducing sugar and is obtained by the partial hydrolysis of starch in presence of the enzyme diastase.
Reason: Hydrolysis of one mole of Maltose gives one mole each of $\alpha-\mathrm{D}-$ Glucose and $\beta-$ D-Fructose.
options: A is correct but R is wrong.
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A .
Both $A$ and $R$ are correct but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$.
questions.solution:
Maltose is a disaccharide composed of two $\alpha$-D-glucose units linked by an $\alpha(1 \to 4)$ glycosidic bond. Since the anomeric carbon of one glucose unit is involved in the glycosidic linkage while the other remains free, it exhibits mutarotation and acts as a reducing sugar. It is indeed produced by the partial hydrolysis of starch using the enzyme diastase. Thus, the Assertion (A) is correct.

Hydrolysis of one mole of maltose yields two moles of $\alpha$-D-glucose, not one mole of glucose and one mole of fructose. The combination of glucose and fructose is characteristic of sucrose. Therefore, the Reason (R) is incorrect.

Answer: A is correct but R is wrong.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Choose the incorrect statement.
options: Denaturation of protein is due to loss of both the secondary and tertiary structures of the protein.
The hormone Glucocorticoid controls the level of excretion of water and salts by the kidney.
Vitamins A and K are fat soluble and are stored in the liver of human beings.
Complete hydrolysis of RNA gives Nitrogen containing bases, a pentose sugar and phosphoric acid.
questions.solution:
Denaturation of proteins involves the loss of secondary and tertiary structures due to physical or chemical changes, while the primary structure remains intact. Thus, the statement regarding denaturation is correct.

Vitamins A, D, E, and K are fat-soluble vitamins and are stored in the liver and adipose tissues. Thus, the statement regarding vitamins is correct.

Complete hydrolysis of RNA yields a pentose sugar (ribose), phosphoric acid, and nitrogenous bases (adenine, guanine, cytosine, and uracil). Thus, the statement regarding RNA hydrolysis is correct.

Glucocorticoids are hormones involved in carbohydrate metabolism, immune response, and inflammation. The hormone that primarily controls the excretion of water and salts by the kidney is mineralocorticoid (specifically aldosterone), not glucocorticoid. Thus, the statement regarding glucocorticoid is incorrect.

Answer: The hormone Glucocorticoid controls the level of excretion of water and salts by the kidney.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the correct statement.
options: The central atoms in both $\mathrm{CH}_4$ and $\mathrm{SF}_4$ are in a state of $\mathrm{sp}^3$ hybridisation
The $\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{O}$ bond length in $\mathrm{CO}_2$ molecule is 110 pm because of the Inductive effect $(+\mathrm{I})$ of oxygen
The resultant dipole moment of $\mathrm{NF}_3$ is greater than that of $\mathrm{NH}_3$
A molecule of the type $\mathrm{AB}_5 \mathrm{E}$ where the central atom has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair has a square pyramid geometry
questions.solution:
(1) Incorrect: C in $CH_4$ is $sp^3$ hybridised (4 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs). S in $SF_4$ has 4 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (steric number 5), making it $sp^3d$ hybridised with a see-saw shape.

(2) Incorrect: Oxygen is highly electronegative and exerts a $-I$ effect (electron-withdrawing), not $+I$.

(3) Incorrect: Dipole moment of $NH_3$ is greater than that of $NF_3$. In $NH_3$, the lone pair dipole and N-H bond dipoles add up. In $NF_3$, the N-F bond dipoles oppose the lone pair dipole, partially canceling it.

(4) Correct: $AB_5E$ type has steric number 6 (octahedral electron geometry). With one lone pair occupying one position, the molecular geometry is square pyramidal (e.g., $BrF_5$, $IF_5$).

The correct statement is (4).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In which one of the following pairs does the stability of the monovalent ion increase with respect to the molecule, while the magnetic character remains the same for both?
questions.solution:
Stability increases when an electron is removed from an antibonding MO (bond order increases). Magnetic character remains the same if both species have the same type (both paramagnetic or both diamagnetic).

(1) $N_2/N_2^+$: $N_2$ — electron removed from bonding $\sigma 2p_z$, BO decreases $3 \to 2.5$. Also $N_2$ is diamagnetic but $N_2^+$ is paramagnetic. Fails both conditions.

(2) $O_2/O_2^+$: $O_2$ — highest occupied MOs are antibonding $\pi^*2p$, BO $= 2$, paramagnetic (2 unpaired electrons). $O_2^+$ — electron removed from $\pi^*$, BO $= 2.5$ (stability increases), 1 unpaired electron — still paramagnetic. Satisfies both conditions.

(3) $C_2/C_2^+$: Electron removed from bonding $\pi 2p$, BO decreases $2 \to 1.5$. Stability decreases.

(4) $B_2/B_2^+$: Electron removed from bonding $\pi 2p$, BO decreases $1 \to 0.5$. Stability decreases.

The correct pair is $O_2/O_2^+$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
From the given covalent compounds (A to F) identify the pair of molecules which have:
(i) Two lone pairs of electrons on the central atom.
(ii) One lone pair of electrons on the central atom.
A. $\mathrm{SO}_2$
B. $\mathrm{ClF}_3$
C. $\mathrm{BF}_3$
D. $\mathrm{BrF}_5$
E. $\mathrm{XeF}_4$
F. $\mathrm{SF}_6$
questions.solution:
The number of lone pairs on the central atom is determined by the formula: Lone pairs = $\dfrac{1}{2}(V - N - C)$, where $V$ is the number of valence electrons of the central atom, $N$ is the number of monovalent atoms bonded to it, and $C$ is the charge on the molecule.

A. $\mathrm{SO}_2$: $V=6$, $N=0$ (oxygen is divalent). Lone pairs = $\dfrac{1}{2}(6 - 0) = 3$ (considering bonding electrons). More accurately, $\mathrm{S}$ has 6 valence electrons, 2 are used for double bonds with each O, leaving 1 lone pair.

B. $\mathrm{ClF}_3$: $V=7$, $N=3$. Lone pairs = $\dfrac{1}{2}(7 - 3) = 2$.

C. $\mathrm{BF}_3$: $V=3$, $N=3$. Lone pairs = $\dfrac{1}{2}(3 - 3) = 0$.

D. $\mathrm{BrF}_5$: $V=7$, $N=5$. Lone pairs = $\dfrac{1}{2}(7 - 5) = 1$.

E. $\mathrm{XeF}_4$: $V=8$, $N=4$. Lone pairs = $\dfrac{1}{2}(8 - 4) = 2$.

F. $\mathrm{SF}_6$: $V=6$, $N=6$. Lone pairs = $\dfrac{1}{2}(6 - 6) = 0$.

Comparing the results:
(i) Two lone pairs: B ($\mathrm{ClF}_3$) and E ($\mathrm{XeF}_4$).
(ii) One lone pair: A ($\mathrm{SO}_2$) and D ($\mathrm{BrF}_5$).

The pair matching (i) is B & E and (ii) is A & D.

Answer: $(i) B \& E \quad (ii) \mathrm{A} \& \mathrm{D}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: $\mathrm{X} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Y}$ is a first order reaction where $1.0 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$ of the reactant yields $0.4 \mathrm{~mol} / \mathrm{L}$ of Y in 200 minutes. Calculate the half-life period of the reaction in minutes.
questions.solution:
The reaction is $\mathrm{X} \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{Y}$.

Let the initial concentration of $\mathrm{X}$ be $[A]_0 = 1.0 \text{ mol/L}$.

At time $t = 200 \text{ minutes}$, the concentration of $\mathrm{Y}$ formed is $0.4 \text{ mol/L}$.

From the stoichiometry, the amount of $\mathrm{X}$ consumed is $\dfrac{1}{2} \times [\mathrm{Y}] = \dfrac{0.4}{2} = 0.2 \text{ mol/L}$.

The concentration of $\mathrm{X}$ remaining at $t = 200 \text{ minutes}$ is $[A]_t = [A]_0 - 0.2 = 1.0 - 0.2 = 0.8 \text{ mol/L}$.

For a first order reaction, the rate constant $k$ is given by $k = \dfrac{2.303}{t} \log \left( \dfrac{[A]_0}{[A]_t} \right)$.

$k = \dfrac{2.303}{200} \log \left( \dfrac{1.0}{0.8} \right) = \dfrac{2.303}{200} \log(1.25) \approx \dfrac{2.303 \times 0.0969}{200} \approx 0.001115 \text{ min}^{-1}$.

The half-life period $t_{1/2}$ is given by $t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{k}$.

$t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.001115} \approx 621.5 \text{ minutes}$.

Answer: $621.5$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two chemical reactions of the same order have equal Frequency factor value.
Their Activation energies differ by $26.8 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$. At 300 K if $k_2=x k_1$ find the value of $x$.
questions.solution:
The Arrhenius equation is given by $k = A e^{-E_a / (RT)}$.

Given that the frequency factors are equal, $A_1 = A_2 = A$.

The rate constants for the two reactions are $k_1 = A e^{-E_{a1} / (RT)}$ and $k_2 = A e^{-E_{a2} / (RT)}$.

Taking the ratio $k_2 / k_1 = e^{(E_{a1} - E_{a2}) / (RT)}$.

Given $E_{a1} - E_{a2} = 26.8 \text{ kJ/mol} = 26800 \text{ J/mol}$, $T = 300 \text{ K}$, and $R = 8.314 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

Substituting the values: $x = k_2 / k_1 = e^{26800 / (8.314 \times 300)}$.

$x = e^{26800 / 2494.2} = e^{10.7449}$.

$x \approx 46397$.

Answer: $4.639 \times 10^4$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The following results were obtained during study of the reaction $2 \mathrm{NO}(\mathrm{g})+\mathrm{Cl}_2(\mathrm{~g}) \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{NOCl}(\mathrm{g})$. Determine the value of $[\mathrm{X}]$ in $\mathrm{mol} / \mathrm{L}\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|} \hline \text{Experiment} & \text{[NO] mol/L} & \left[\mathrm{Cl}_2\right] \text{ mol/L} & \text{Initial rate of formation. [NOCl] mol/L/min} \\ \hline \text{I} & 0.2 & 0.2 & 6.0 \times 10^{-3} \\ \hline \text{II} & 0.2 & 0.4 & 2.4 \times 10^{-2} \\ \hline \text{III} & 0.4 & 0.2 & 1.2 \times 10^{-2} \\ \hline \text{IV} & X & 0.6 & 1.35 \times 10^{-1} \\ \hline \end{array}$
questions.solution:
The rate law for the reaction $2 \mathrm{NO}(g) + \mathrm{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2 \mathrm{NOCl}(g)$ is given by $r = k[\mathrm{NO}]^a[\mathrm{Cl}_2]^b$.

From experiment I and II, keeping $[\mathrm{NO}]$ constant at $0.2 \text{ mol/L}$:
$\dfrac{2.4 \times 10^{-2}}{6.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \left( \dfrac{0.4}{0.2} \right)^b \Rightarrow 4 = 2^b \Rightarrow b = 2$.

From experiment I and III, keeping $[\mathrm{Cl}_2]$ constant at $0.2 \text{ mol/L}$:
$\dfrac{1.2 \times 10^{-2}}{6.0 \times 10^{-3}} = \left( \dfrac{0.4}{0.2} \right)^a \Rightarrow 2 = 2^a \Rightarrow a = 1$.

The rate law is $r = k[\mathrm{NO}][\mathrm{Cl}_2]^2$.

Using experiment I to find $k$:
$6.0 \times 10^{-3} = k(0.2)(0.2)^2 = k(0.2)(0.04) = k(0.008)$.
$k = \dfrac{6.0 \times 10^{-3}}{8.0 \times 10^{-3}} = 0.75 \text{ L}^2 \text{ mol}^{-2} \text{ min}^{-1}$.

For experiment IV:
$1.35 \times 10^{-1} = 0.75 \times [X] \times (0.6)^2$.
$0.135 = 0.75 \times [X] \times 0.36$.
$0.135 = 0.27 \times [X]$.
$[X] = \dfrac{0.135}{0.27} = 0.5 \text{ mol/L}$.

Answer: $[\mathrm{X}]=0.5$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Two statements, One Assertion (A) and the other Reason (R) are given. Choose the right option.
Assertion: The rate constant $(\mathrm{k})$ for a chemical reaction gets nearly doubled for a $10^{\circ}$ rise in temperature.
Reason: The number of bimolecular collisions between reactant molecules increase with increase in temperature
options: A is wrong but $R$ is correct.
Both $A$ and $R$ are correct but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$.
Both $A$ and $R$ are correct and $R$ is the correct explanation of $A$.
A is correct but R is wrong.
questions.solution:
The rate constant $k$ of a reaction is given by the Arrhenius equation $k = A e^{-E_a / RT}$. For most reactions, a $10^{\circ}C$ rise in temperature leads to a doubling or tripling of the rate constant. This is primarily due to the increase in the fraction of molecules possessing energy greater than or equal to the activation energy $E_a$, which is represented by the term $e^{-E_a / RT}$.

The number of bimolecular collisions between reactant molecules does increase with an increase in temperature because the average kinetic energy and velocity of the molecules increase. However, the increase in the total number of collisions is proportional to $\sqrt{T}$, which is very small compared to the exponential increase in the fraction of effective collisions (those with energy $\ge E_a$).

Therefore, while both statements are factually correct, the increase in the number of collisions is not the primary reason for the doubling of the rate constant; the primary reason is the exponential increase in the fraction of molecules with energy greater than the activation energy. Thus, R is not the correct explanation of A.

Answer: Both $A$ and $R$ are correct but $R$ is not the correct explanation of $A$.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a given reaction of the type $\dfrac{3}{5} X(a q) \rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2} Y(a q)+Z(g)$, the correct expression for the rate of disappearance of $X$ with reference to $Y$ is $\qquad$
questions.solution:
For a general chemical reaction $aA + bB \rightarrow cC + dD$, the rate of reaction is given by $-\dfrac{1}{a} \dfrac{d[A]}{dt} = -\dfrac{1}{b} \dfrac{d[B]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{c} \dfrac{d[C]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{d} \dfrac{d[D]}{dt}$.

Given the reaction $\dfrac{3}{5} X \rightarrow \dfrac{1}{2} Y + Z$, we apply the rate expression:

$-\dfrac{1}{3/5} \dfrac{d[X]}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{1/2} \dfrac{d[Y]}{dt}$

$-\dfrac{5}{3} \dfrac{d[X]}{dt} = 2 \dfrac{d[Y]}{dt}$

Rearranging to solve for the rate of disappearance of $X$, which is $-\dfrac{d[X]}{dt}$:

$-\dfrac{d[X]}{dt} = \dfrac{3}{5} \times 2 \dfrac{d[Y]}{dt}$

$-\dfrac{d[X]}{dt} = \dfrac{6}{5} \dfrac{d[Y]}{dt}$

Answer: $-d \dfrac{[X]}{d t}=+\dfrac{6}{5} d \dfrac{[Y]}{d t}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.chapter: Classification of Elements and Periodicity in Properties
questions.q:
Choose the pair of elements $[(A)$ to $(F)]$ which:
(i) belong to the Chalcogen family
(ii) form monovalent oxides which give alkalies in aqueous solution
(iii) form stable monovalent anions

$(A)1 s^2 2 s^2 2 p^6 3 s^2 3 p^6 4 s^1  \quad (B) 1 s^2 2 s^2 2 p^5  \quad (C) 1 s^2 2 s^2 2 p^6 3 s^1  \quad 
(D) 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^6 3 \mathrm{~s}^2 3 \mathrm{p}^5  \quad (E) 1 s^2 2 s^2 2 p^6 3 s^2 3 p^4  \quad (F) 1 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{~s}^2 2 \mathrm{p}^4$
questions.solution:
Identifying each element by valence configuration:

A ($4s^1$) \rightarrow Group 1 (Alkali metal)
B ($2s^22p^5$) \rightarrow Group 17 (Halogen)
C ($3s^1$) \rightarrow Group 1 (Alkali metal)
D ($3s^23p^5$) \rightarrow Group 17 (Halogen)
E ($3s^23p^4$) \rightarrow Group 16 (Chalcogen)
F ($2p^4$) \rightarrow Group 16 (Chalcogen)

(i) Chalcogen family (Group 16): E and F

(ii) Monovalent oxides giving alkalies (Group 1, $ns^1$): A and C (form $Na_2O$, $K_2O$ type oxides \rightarrow alkaline solution)

(iii) Stable monovalent anions (Group 17, need 1 electron): B and D

Answer: (i) E&F, (ii) A&C, (iii) B&D

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An aqueous solution of $\mathrm{CrCl}_3 .6 \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ (Molar mass $=266.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ ) containing 2.665 g of the solute after processing, when treated with excess of $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ gave 2.87 g of AgCl (Molar mass of $\mathrm{AgCl}=143.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ ) Choose the correct formula of the compound which give these results.
questions.solution:
The number of moles of the complex $\mathrm{CrCl}_3 \cdot 6\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ is calculated as:
Moles of complex $= \dfrac{2.665 \text{ g}}{266.5 \text{ g/mol}} = 0.01 \text{ mol}$.

The number of moles of $\mathrm{AgCl}$ precipitated is calculated as:
Moles of $\mathrm{AgCl} = \dfrac{2.87 \text{ g}}{143.5 \text{ g/mol}} = 0.02 \text{ mol}$.

The reaction with $\mathrm{AgNO}_3$ precipitates only the chloride ions present outside the coordination sphere. Let $x$ be the number of ionizable chloride ions per mole of the complex. The stoichiometry of the reaction is:
Moles of $\mathrm{AgCl} = x \times \text{Moles of complex}$
$0.02 = x \times 0.01$
$x = 2$.

Since there are 2 ionizable chloride ions, the formula must contain 2 chloride ions outside the coordination sphere. Among the given options, $\left[\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O})_5\mathrm{Cl}\right]\mathrm{Cl}_2 \cdot \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$ satisfies this condition.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{Cr}\left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}\right] \mathrm{Cl}_2 \cdot \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which one of the following coordination compounds will exhibit both geometrical and optical isomerism?
questions.solution:
The complex $\left[\mathrm{Cr}(\mathrm{ox})_3\right]^{3-}$ is a tris-chelated complex of the form $M(AA)_3$. It exhibits optical isomerism but does not show geometrical isomerism because all donor atoms are identical.

The complex $[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{CN})_6]^{3-}$ is an octahedral complex of the form $MA_6$. It does not exhibit either geometrical or optical isomerism.

The complex $\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{en})_2 \mathrm{Cl}_2\right]^{+}$ is of the form $M(AA)_2 a_2$. The cis-isomer of this complex is optically active (chiral) and also exists as a geometrical isomer (cis and trans). The trans-isomer is optically inactive due to the presence of a plane of symmetry. Since the cis-isomer exhibits both geometrical (relative to trans) and optical isomerism, this complex satisfies the condition.

The complex $\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{NO}_3)_3(\mathrm{NH}_3)_3\right]$ is of the form $Ma_3b_3$. It exhibits geometrical isomerism (fac and mer isomers) but does not exhibit optical isomerism as both isomers possess planes of symmetry.

Answer: $\left[\mathrm{Co}(\mathrm{en})_2 \mathrm{Cl}_2\right]^{+}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Arrange the following compounds in the decreasing order of the molar conductivities of their aqueous solutions.
$\begin{array}{cccc}\mathrm{A} & \quad \mathrm{B} & \quad \mathrm{C} & \quad \mathrm{D} \\ {\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_5 \mathrm{Cl}] \mathrm{Cl}_2\right.} & \quad {\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_3 \mathrm{Cl}_3\right]} & \quad {\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_4 \mathrm{Cl}_2\right] \mathrm{Cl}} & \quad {\left[\mathrm{Co}\left(\mathrm{NH}_3\right)_6\right] \mathrm{Cl}_3}\end{array}$
questions.solution:
Molar conductivity of an electrolyte in aqueous solution depends on the number of ions produced upon dissociation. The greater the number of ions, the higher the molar conductivity.

Dissociation of the given complexes:
A: $[Co(NH_3)_5Cl]Cl_2 \rightarrow [Co(NH_3)_5Cl]^{2+} + 2Cl^{-}$. Total ions = 3.
B: $[Co(NH_3)_3Cl_3] \rightarrow [Co(NH_3)_3Cl_3]$. Total ions = 0 (non-electrolyte).
C: $[Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]Cl \rightarrow [Co(NH_3)_4Cl_2]^{+} + Cl^{-}$. Total ions = 2.
D: $[Co(NH_3)_6]Cl_3 \rightarrow [Co(NH_3)_6]^{3+} + 3Cl^{-}$. Total ions = 4.

Comparing the number of ions produced:
D (4 ions) > A (3 ions) > C (2 ions) > B (0 ions).

Therefore, the decreasing order of molar conductivity is D > A > C > B.

Answer: $D \gt A \gt C \gt B$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match the coordination compounds in Column I having the given type of hybridisation of $\mathrm{M}^{\mathrm{n}+}$ ion and magnetic moment as given in Column II.
\(\begin{array}{|l|l|l|l|} \hline & \text { Coordination compounds. } & & \text { Hybridisation \& Magnetic nature. } \\ \hline \text { A } & \mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CO})_4 & \text { P } & \mathrm{sp}^3, \quad \mu=5.92 \mathrm{BM} \\ \hline \text { B } & {\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{CN})_4\right]^{2-}} & \text { Q } & \mathrm{sp}^3, \quad \mu=2.84 \mathrm{BM} \\ \hline \text { C } & {\left[\mathrm{Ni}(\mathrm{Cl})_4\right]^{2-}} & \text { R } & \mathrm{sp}^3, \quad \mu=0 \\ \hline \text { D } & {[\mathrm{MnBr}]^{2-}} & \text { S } & \mathrm{dsp}^2, \quad \mu=0 \\ \hline \end{array}\)
questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{Ni(CO)_4}$, the oxidation state of Ni is 0. The electronic configuration is $[Ar] 3d^8 4s^2$. Since CO is a strong field ligand, it causes pairing of electrons, leading to $sp^3$ hybridization. All electrons are paired, so $\mu = 0$. This matches R.

For $[Ni(CN)_4]^{2-}$, the oxidation state of Ni is +2. The electronic configuration is $[Ar] 3d^8$. CN$^-$ is a strong field ligand, causing pairing of electrons in the $3d$ orbitals, resulting in $dsp^2$ hybridization. All electrons are paired, so $\mu = 0$. This matches S.

For $[Ni(Cl)_4]^{2-}$, the oxidation state of Ni is +2. The electronic configuration is $[Ar] 3d^8$. Cl$^-$ is a weak field ligand, so no pairing occurs. The hybridization is $sp^3$ with two unpaired electrons. The magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{2(2+2)} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.84$ BM. This matches Q.

For $[MnBr_4]^{2-}$, the oxidation state of Mn is +2. The electronic configuration is $[Ar] 3d^5$. Br$^-$ is a weak field ligand, so no pairing occurs. The hybridization is $sp^3$ with five unpaired electrons. The magnetic moment is $\mu = \sqrt{5(5+2)} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92$ BM. This matches P.

Answer: $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{R} \quad \mathrm{B}=\mathrm{S} \quad \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{Q} \quad \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{P}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the spin only magnetic moment of the metal ion in $\mathrm{P}$ and the oxidation number of Sulphur in the oxidised product $\mathrm{Z}$ ?
questions.solution:
Pyrolusite is $MnO_2$. When fused with $KOH$ and $KNO_3$, it forms potassium manganate ($K_2MnO_4$), which is compound $P$.

$2MnO_2 + 4KOH + O_2 \rightarrow 2K_2MnO_4 + 2H_2O$.

In $K_2MnO_4$, the manganese ion is $MnO_4^{2-}$. The oxidation state of $Mn$ is $+6$. The electronic configuration of $Mn^{6+}$ is $[Ar] 3d^1$.

The number of unpaired electrons $n = 1$. The spin-only magnetic moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{1(1+2)} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732 \text{ BM}$.

Compound $P$ ($K_2MnO_4$) undergoes disproportionation in acidic medium to form $MnO_2$ (blackish brown, $X$) and $KMnO_4$ ($Y$).

$3MnO_4^{2-} + 4H^+ \rightarrow 2MnO_4^- + MnO_2 + 2H_2O$.

Thus, $Y$ is $MnO_4^-$. In neutral medium, $MnO_4^-$ reacts with thiosulphate $(S_2O_3)^{2-}$ to form $MnO_2$ and sulphate $(SO_4)^{2-}$.

$8MnO_4^- + 3S_2O_3^{2-} + H_2O \rightarrow 8MnO_2 + 6SO_4^{2-} + 2OH^-$.

The oxidised product $Z$ is $SO_4^{2-}$. In $SO_4^{2-}$, the oxidation number of sulphur is calculated as $x + 4(-2) = -2$, which gives $x = +6$.

Answer: $\mu=1.732 \mathrm{BM} \quad$ Oxidation number $=+6$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Match the metals in Column II with their characteristic properties given in Column I.
\(\begin{array}{|c|l|c|c|} \hline & \text { Properties } & & \text { Metals } \\ \hline \text { A } & \text { Lanthanoid with low value of } 3^{\text {rd }} \text { ionisation enthalpy. } & P & V \\ \hline \text { B } & \text { f-Block element with electronic configuration }[\mathrm{Rn}] 6 \mathrm{~d}^2 7 \mathrm{~s}^2 & Q & G d \\ \hline \text { C } & 3 \mathrm{~d} \text {-series metal whose } \mathrm{M}^{3+}{ }_{(\mathrm{aq})} \text { is colourless. } & R & T h \\ \hline \text { D } & 3 \mathrm{~d} \text {-series metal with highest } \Delta \mathrm{H}_{(\text {atomisation })} & S & S c \\ \hline \end{array}\)
questions.solution:
A: Gadolinium (Gd) has the electronic configuration $[Xe] 4f^7 5d^1 6s^2$. The removal of the third electron from the $5d$ orbital is relatively easy because it results in a stable half-filled $4f^7$ configuration. Thus, Gd has a low third ionisation enthalpy. So, A = Q.

B: Thorium (Th) is an actinoid with the electronic configuration $[Rn] 6d^2 7s^2$. So, B = R.

C: Scandium (Sc) is a $3d$-series metal with the electronic configuration $[Ar] 3d^1 4s^2$. Its $Sc^{3+}$ ion has the configuration $[Ar]$, which has no $d$-electrons ($d^0$). Therefore, $Sc^{3+}_{(aq)}$ is colourless. So, C = S.

D: Vanadium (V) is a $3d$-series metal. Among the given choices, Vanadium has a high enthalpy of atomisation due to the presence of unpaired electrons in the $d$-orbitals, which contribute to strong metallic bonding. So, D = P.

Combining these, we get A = Q, B = R, C = S, D = P.

Answer: $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{Q} \quad \mathrm{B}=\mathrm{R} \quad \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{S} \quad \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{P}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Choose the correct statement.
options: Ionic compounds of $\mathrm{Sc}^{3+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu}^{+}$are coloured because of $\mathrm{d}-\mathrm{d}$ electronic transitions

The order in which the paramagnetic nature of the 4 cations $\mathrm{Cr}^{2+}, \mathrm{Mn}^{2+}, \mathrm{V}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ vary is $\mathrm{V}^{2+} \lt \mathrm{Cr}^{2+}=\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} \lt \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$
The metal Cobalt has the electronic configuration $[\mathrm{Ar}] 3 \mathrm{~d}^5$ in the +3 oxidation state
As the oxidation number of the transition element increases, the ionic nature decreases and the oxides show acidic nature predominantly
questions.solution:
(1) Incorrect: $Sc^{3+}$ has $[Ar]3d^0$ and $Cu^+$ has $[Ar]3d^{10}$. With completely empty or completely filled $d$-orbitals, $d$-$d$ transitions are not possible. Their compounds are colourless.

(2) Incorrect: Paramagnetism depends on number of unpaired electrons $n$.
$V^{2+}(3d^3) \to n=3$, $Cr^{2+}(3d^4) \to n=4$, $Mn^{2+}(3d^5) \to n=5$, $Fe^{2+}(3d^6) \to n=4$
Correct order: $V^{2+} \lt Cr^{2+} = Fe^{2+} \lt Mn^{2+}$

(3) Incorrect: Co is $[Ar]3d^74s^2$. In $+3$ state ($Co^{3+}$), it loses $2$ electrons from $4s$ and $1$ from $3d$, giving $[Ar]3d^6$, not $3d^5$.

(4) Correct: By Fajans' rules, higher oxidation state increases polarizing power, increasing covalent character and decreasing ionic nature. Higher covalent character in oxides leads to predominantly acidic nature (e.g., $CrO_3$, $Mn_2O_7$ are acidic while $MnO$, $CrO$ are basic).

The correct statement is (4).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The EMF of the cell $\mathrm{Al} / \mathrm{Al}^{3+}(0.01 \mathrm{M}) \| \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(0.02 \mathrm{M}) / \mathrm{Fe}$ is 1.209 V . The EMF of the cell can be increased by ------------------------------
questions.solution:
The cell reaction is $2\mathrm{Al}(s) + 3\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Al}^{3+}(aq) + 3\mathrm{Fe}(s)$.

The Nernst equation for the cell EMF is given by $E_{cell} = E^{0}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log Q$, where $Q = \dfrac{[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]^3}$ and $n = 6$.

Substituting the expression for $Q$: $E_{cell} = E^{0}_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0591}{6} \log \left( \dfrac{[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]^3} \right)$.

To increase $E_{cell}$, the value of the term $\log \left( \dfrac{[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]^2}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]^3} \right)$ must be decreased. This can be achieved by either decreasing the numerator $[\mathrm{Al}^{3+}]$ or increasing the denominator $[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]$.

Among the given options, increasing the concentration of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ will decrease the value of $Q$, thereby increasing the EMF of the cell.

Answer: increasing the concentration of $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
The conductivity of 0.01 M solution of $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$ at 298 K is $1.65 \times 10^{-4} \mathrm{Scm}^{-1}$
What is the $\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{a}}$ value of the acid if $\lambda^0\left(\mathrm{H}^{+}\right)$and $\lambda^0\left(\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COO}\right)^{-1}$ are $349.1 \mathrm{Scm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ and $40.9 \mathrm{Scm}^2 \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ respectively?
questions.solution:
The molar conductivity $\Lambda_m$ is given by the formula $\Lambda_m = \dfrac{\kappa \times 1000}{C}$, where $\kappa = 1.65 \times 10^{-4} \text{ S cm}^{-1}$ and $C = 0.01 \text{ M}$.

$\Lambda_m = \dfrac{1.65 \times 10^{-4} \times 1000}{0.01} = 16.5 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

The limiting molar conductivity $\Lambda_m^0$ is $\lambda^0(\text{H}^+) + \lambda^0(\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-) = 349.1 + 40.9 = 390.0 \text{ S cm}^2 \text{ mol}^{-1}$.

The degree of dissociation $\alpha$ is given by $\alpha = \dfrac{\Lambda_m}{\Lambda_m^0} = \dfrac{16.5}{390.0} \approx 0.0423$.

The dissociation constant $K_a$ is given by $K_a = \dfrac{C\alpha^2}{1 - \alpha}$. Since $\alpha$ is small, $1 - \alpha \approx 1$.

$K_a \approx C\alpha^2 = 0.01 \times (0.0423)^2 = 0.01 \times 0.001789 = 1.789 \times 10^{-5}$.

The $\text{pK}_a$ value is $-\log_{10}(K_a) = -\log_{10}(1.789 \times 10^{-5}) = 5 - \log_{10}(1.789) \approx 5 - 0.2526 = 4.747$.

Answer: $4.75$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
What is the reduction potential of a half-cell consisting of a Pt electrode dipped in $2.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ and $0.04 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ solution where the reaction taking place is conversion of $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ ions to $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ ?
$\mathrm{E}^0\left(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} / \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\right)=0.771 \mathrm{~V}$
questions.solution:
The reduction half-reaction is given by $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+} + e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$.

Using the Nernst equation for the electrode potential at $298 \mathrm{K}$:

$E = E^{0} - \dfrac{0.0591}{n} \log \dfrac{[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}]}{[\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}]}$

Given $E^{0} = 0.771 \mathrm{V}$, $n = 1$, $[\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}] = 2.2 \mathrm{M}$, and $[\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}] = 0.04 \mathrm{M}$.

Substituting the values:

$E = 0.771 - \dfrac{0.0591}{1} \log \left( \dfrac{2.2}{0.04} \right)$

$E = 0.771 - 0.0591 \log(55)$

Since $\log(55) \approx 1.74036$:

$E = 0.771 - 0.0591 \times 1.74036$

$E = 0.771 - 0.10285$

$E \approx 0.66815 \mathrm{V}$

Answer: 0.668 V

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A current of 2.5 amperes is passed through 800 ml of 0.48 M solution of $\mathrm{CuSO}_4$ for 1.0 hour with a current efficiency of $80 \%$. If the volume of the solution remains unchanged, what is the final molarity of the solution?
questions.solution:
The reaction at the cathode is $\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^{-} \rightarrow \text{Cu}(s)$.

The total charge passed through the solution is $Q = I \times t \times \text{efficiency} = 2.5 \text{ A} \times (1.0 \times 3600 \text{ s}) \times 0.80 = 7200 \text{ C}$.

The number of moles of electrons transferred is $n_{e} = \dfrac{Q}{F} = \dfrac{7200}{96500} \approx 0.07461 \text{ mol}$.

Since 2 moles of electrons are required to reduce 1 mole of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions, the moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ consumed is $n_{\text{Cu}^{2+}} = \dfrac{n_{e}}{2} = \dfrac{0.07461}{2} = 0.037305 \text{ mol}$.

The initial moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ in 800 ml (0.8 L) of 0.48 M solution is $n_{\text{initial}} = 0.48 \text{ M} \times 0.8 \text{ L} = 0.384 \text{ mol}$.

The final moles of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ remaining is $n_{\text{final}} = 0.384 - 0.037305 = 0.346695 \text{ mol}$.

The final molarity is $M_{\text{final}} = \dfrac{n_{\text{final}}}{V} = \dfrac{0.346695}{0.8} \approx 0.43336 \text{ M}$.

Answer: $0.433$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Match the structures in Column I with their correct IUPAC names given in Column II.
questions.solution:
Structure A shows a benzene ring substituted at the 4-position with an isobutyl group and at the 1-position with a propanoic acid group. The IUPAC name is 2-(4-isobutylphenyl)propanoic acid, which matches R.

Structure B shows a propane chain with three carboxylic acid groups at positions 1, 2, and 3, and a hydroxyl group at position 2. The IUPAC name is 2-hydroxypropane-1,2,3-tricarboxylic acid, which matches S.

Structure C shows a hexanedial chain with bromine atoms at positions 2 and 3. The IUPAC name is 2,3-dibromohexanedial, which matches Q.

Structure D shows a pentane chain with a phenyl group at position 1 and bromine atoms at positions 2 and 3. The IUPAC name is 2,3-dibromo-1-phenylpentane, which matches P.

Therefore, the correct matching is A=R, B=S, C=Q, D=P.

Answer: $\mathrm{A}=\mathrm{R} \quad \mathrm{B}=\mathrm{S} \quad \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{Q} \quad \mathrm{D}=\mathrm{P}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Arrange the following free radicals in the increasing order of their stability:
questions.solution:
The stability of free radicals is primarily determined by resonance, hyperconjugation, and the inductive effect.

Structure A is an isopropyl radical, which is a secondary ($2^{\circ}$) alkyl radical. It is stabilized by hyperconjugation from 6 $\alpha$-hydrogens.

Structure B is a tert-butyl radical, which is a tertiary ($3^{\circ}$) alkyl radical. It is stabilized by hyperconjugation from 9 $\alpha$-hydrogens. Thus, B is more stable than A.

Structure C is an allyl radical ($CH_2=CH-CH_2^{\bullet}$), which is stabilized by resonance. The unpaired electron is delocalized over the $\pi$ system. Resonance stabilization is generally more significant than hyperconjugation.

Structure D is a benzyl radical ($C_6H_5-CH_2^{\bullet}$), which is stabilized by resonance with the benzene ring. The unpaired electron is delocalized over the entire aromatic ring, providing greater resonance stabilization than the allyl radical.

Comparing the stability:
1. Alkyl radicals (A and B) are less stable than resonance-stabilized radicals (C and D).
2. Among alkyl radicals, $3^{\circ} \gt 2^{\circ}$, so $B \gt A$.
3. Among resonance-stabilized radicals, the benzyl radical (D) is more stable than the allyl radical (C) due to more extensive delocalization.

Therefore, the increasing order of stability is $A \lt B \lt C \lt D$.

Answer: $\mathrm{A} \lt \mathrm{B} \lt \mathrm{C} \lt \mathrm{D}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which one of the following is a true statement with reference to reaction between 2- Bromo-2-methylpropane and aqueous KOH ?
options: The reaction is not favoured by the presence of polar protic solvent.
The reaction occurs at a slow rate since it follows $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}} 2$ mechanism.
The reaction occurs at a fast rate since the substrate is a tertiary alkyl halide and follows $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ mechanism.
The rate of reaction depends on the concentration of the haloalkane and the nucleophile $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$
questions.solution:
The substrate 2-bromo-2-methylpropane is a tertiary alkyl halide. Tertiary alkyl halides undergo nucleophilic substitution primarily via the $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}1$ mechanism because the carbocation intermediate formed is highly stable due to inductive and hyperconjugation effects.

The $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}1$ mechanism involves the rate-determining step of carbocation formation, which is independent of the concentration of the nucleophile. Thus, the rate law is given by $\text{Rate} = k[\text{Substrate}]$.

Polar protic solvents stabilize the carbocation intermediate and the leaving group through solvation, thereby facilitating the $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}1$ reaction.

Comparing the options, the statement that the reaction occurs at a fast rate because the substrate is a tertiary alkyl halide following the $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}1$ mechanism is correct, as the stability of the tertiary carbocation allows for a relatively rapid formation compared to primary or secondary substrates in the same mechanism.

Answer: The reaction occurs at a fast rate since the substrate is a tertiary alkyl halide and follows $\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}} 1$ mechanism.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which of the following haloalkanes will give more than one isomeric product, on being heated with alc. KOH ?
questions.solution:
Dehydrohalogenation of haloalkanes with alcoholic KOH follows Saytzeff rule, where the major product is the more substituted alkene. If multiple distinct $\beta$-hydrogens are available such that different alkenes can be formed, isomeric products are obtained.

For 1-chloro-2-methylbutane ($CH_3CH_2CH(CH_3)CH_2Cl$), the only $\beta$-hydrogen is on the carbon at position 2, leading to 2-methyl-1-butene. Only one product is formed.

For 2-chlorobutane ($CH_3CH_2CHClCH_3$), $\beta$-hydrogens are present on C1 and C3. Elimination from C1 gives but-1-ene, and elimination from C3 gives but-2-ene (cis and trans isomers). Thus, multiple isomeric products are formed.

For 2-chloro-3,3-dimethylpentane ($CH_3CHClC(CH_3)_2CH_2CH_3$), $\beta$-hydrogens are present on C1 and C3. However, C3 has no hydrogens, so elimination can only occur towards C1, yielding 3,3-dimethylpent-2-ene. Only one product is formed.

For 1-chloropentane ($CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2Cl$), the only $\beta$-hydrogen is on C2, leading to pent-1-ene. Only one product is formed.

Answer: 2- Chlorobutane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Both reactions (i) and (ii) give the same compound X as the major product. Identify X
(i). 3-Methylbut-1-ene $+\mathrm{HCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{X}$
(ii). Neopentyl alcohol $+\mathrm{HCl}\left(\right.$ anh. $\left.\mathrm{ZnCl}_2\right) \rightarrow \mathrm{X}$
questions.solution:
In reaction (i), the electrophilic addition of $\mathrm{HCl}$ to 3-methylbut-1-ene proceeds via the formation of a carbocation. The initial protonation of the double bond yields the secondary carbocation $(CH_3)_2CH-CH^{+}-CH_3$. This secondary carbocation undergoes a 1,2-hydride shift to form the more stable tertiary carbocation $(CH_3)_2C^{+}-CH_2-CH_3$. Subsequent attack by the chloride ion gives the major product $X$ as 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, which is $(CH_3)_2CCl-CH_2-CH_3$.

In reaction (ii), the reaction of neopentyl alcohol $(CH_3)_3C-CH_2OH$ with $\mathrm{HCl}$ and anhydrous $\mathrm{ZnCl}_2$ (Lucas reagent) involves the formation of a carbocation. The protonated alcohol loses water to form the primary neopentyl carbocation $(CH_3)_3C-CH_2^{+}$. This primary carbocation is highly unstable and undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to rearrange into the more stable tertiary carbocation $(CH_3)_2C^{+}-CH_2-CH_3$. The chloride ion then attacks this tertiary carbocation to yield the same major product $X$, which is 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, $(CH_3)_2CCl-CH_2-CH_3$.

Answer: $\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2-\mathrm{CCl}_{-}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the final product $[Z]$ formed when Chlorobenzene undergoes the given series of reactions:
questions.solution:
The reaction sequence begins with the Friedel-Crafts alkylation of chlorobenzene with methyl chloride in the presence of anhydrous $AlCl_{3}$. Chlorobenzene is ortho/para directing, and the para-isomer is the major product due to steric hindrance at the ortho position. Thus, $[W]$ is 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene (p-chlorotoluene).

Next, $[W]$ reacts with $Cl_{2}$ in the presence of UV light. This is a free-radical substitution reaction that occurs at the benzylic position. Therefore, $[X]$ is 1-chloro-4-(chloromethyl)benzene (p-chlorobenzyl chloride).

Then, $[X]$ reacts with alcoholic $KCN$ and heat. This is a nucleophilic substitution reaction where the benzylic chloride is replaced by a cyanide group, yielding $[Y]$, which is 2-(4-chlorophenyl)acetonitrile.

Finally, the hydrolysis of the nitrile $[Y]$ with excess dilute $HCl$ converts the $-CN$ group into a carboxylic acid group $-COOH$. Thus, the final product $[Z]$ is 2-(4-chlorophenyl)acetic acid, which corresponds to the structure shown in the first option.

Answer:

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the final product $[Z]$ formed when the given reactions take place?
questions.solution:
The reaction of phenol with Zn dust under heating conditions leads to the reduction of phenol to benzene. Thus, [X] is benzene ($C_{6}H_{6}$).

The reaction of benzene with a mixture of concentrated $HNO_{3}$ and concentrated $H_{2}SO_{4}$ (nitrating mixture) results in electrophilic aromatic substitution, specifically nitration, to form nitrobenzene. Thus, [Y] is nitrobenzene ($C_{6}H_{5}NO_{2}$).

The reaction of nitrobenzene with $Br_{2}$ in the presence of $FeBr_{3}$ is an electrophilic aromatic substitution. The nitro group ($-NO_{2}$) is a strongly deactivating group and is meta-directing. Therefore, the bromine atom will be substituted at the meta position relative to the nitro group. Thus, [Z] is 3-bromonitrobenzene (also known as m-bromonitrobenzene).

Answer: 3-Bromonitrobenzene.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An unsaturated hydrocarbon $[\mathrm{A}]$ undergoes the following series of reactions. Identify $[\mathrm{A}]$.
questions.solution:
The hydrocarbon [A] reacts with ammoniacal $AgNO_3$ to give no reaction, which indicates that it is not a terminal alkyne. This eliminates but-1-yne and propyne.

The reaction of [A] with $Na/liquid NH_3$ gives a trans product, which is a characteristic reaction of internal alkynes to form trans-alkenes. This suggests [A] is an internal alkyne.

The reaction of [A] with alkaline $KMnO_4$ at 383 K yields 2 moles of a carboxylic acid with formula $C_2H_4O_2$, which is acetic acid ($CH_3COOH$). This implies that the oxidative cleavage of the triple bond in [A] produces two molecules of acetic acid. For an internal alkyne $R-C \equiv C-R$ to yield two molecules of $CH_3COOH$, the structure must be $CH_3-C \equiv C-CH_3$, which is but-2-yne.

Ozonolysis of but-2-yne ($CH_3-C \equiv C-CH_3$) followed by $Zn/H_2O$ yields a diketone, specifically butane-2,3-dione ($CH_3COCOCH_3$), which matches the description of [B].

Therefore, [A] is but-2-yne.

Answer: But-2-yne

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which one of the following statements is correct?
options: The Electrophilic addition to an unsymmetrical alkene always occurs through the formation of a more stable Carbanion intermediate.

Between the two alkenes - (i) $\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2-\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3$ and (ii). $\mathrm{C}_6 \mathrm{H}_5-\mathrm{CH}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_3$, compound (i) will show geometrical isomerism
Greater the number of alkyl groups attached to the double bonded Carbon atoms, the less stable is the alkene.
The major product formed when 2-Methylpropene reacts with dilute $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$ is tert. butyl alcohol.
questions.solution:
Electrophilic addition to an unsymmetrical alkene proceeds via the formation of a more stable carbocation intermediate, not a carbanion. Thus, the first statement is incorrect.

For geometrical isomerism, each carbon atom of the double bond must be attached to two different groups. In compound (i), $\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2 \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_3$, the carbon atom on the left is attached to two identical methyl groups, so it does not show geometrical isomerism. Thus, the second statement is incorrect.

According to the stability of alkenes, the stability increases with the number of alkyl groups attached to the double-bonded carbon atoms due to hyperconjugation and inductive effects. Thus, the third statement is incorrect.

When 2-methylpropene, $\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_2 \mathrm{C}=\mathrm{CH}_2$, reacts with dilute $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$, the reaction follows Markovnikov's rule. The proton adds to the terminal carbon to form the more stable tert-butyl carbocation, $\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3 \mathrm{C}^{+}$, which then reacts with water to form tert-butyl alcohol, $\left(\mathrm{CH}_3\right)_3 \mathrm{COH}$. Thus, the fourth statement is correct.

Answer: The major product formed when 2-Methylpropene reacts with dilute $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$ is tert. butyl alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Convert Benzene \rightarrow  3-Bromophenol by choosing appropriate reagents $[(i)$ to (v)] in the correct sequence.
$(i)\mathrm{NaNO}_2 / \mathrm{HCl}\left(0^{\circ} \mathrm{C}\right)  \quad (ii) Conc. \mathrm{HNO}_3 / \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4  \quad (iii) \mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O} / 283 \mathrm{~K}  \quad (iv) \mathrm{Fe} / \mathrm{HCl}  \quad (v) \mathrm{Br} 2 / \mathrm{Fe}$
questions.solution:
The conversion of benzene to 3-bromophenol requires the introduction of a meta-directing group followed by bromination, or the use of a group that directs meta and can be converted to a hydroxyl group. Since the hydroxyl group is ortho/para-directing, it must be introduced after the bromine atom is placed in the meta position.

Nitration of benzene using $Conc. HNO_3 / H_2SO_4$ (reagent ii) gives nitrobenzene.

Bromination of nitrobenzene using $Br_2 / Fe$ (reagent v) gives 1-bromo-3-nitrobenzene because the nitro group is meta-directing.

Reduction of the nitro group using $Fe / HCl$ (reagent iv) gives 3-bromoaniline.

Diazotization of 3-bromoaniline using $NaNO_2 / HCl$ at $0^{\circ}C$ (reagent i) gives 3-bromobenzenediazonium chloride.

Hydrolysis of the diazonium salt using $H_2O / 283 K$ (reagent iii) gives 3-bromophenol.

The correct sequence is ii, v, iv, i, iii.

Answer: ii, v, iv, i, iii

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Identify the compound which gives an optically active haloalkane on reaction with $\mathrm{H}_2$ / Ni on heating.
questions.solution:
$H_2$/Ni reduces the double bond to give a haloalkane. The product is optically active only if it contains a chiral centre (4 different groups on the Cl-bearing carbon).

A (3-chloropent-1-ene): Reduction gives 3-chloropentane. Cl-bearing carbon has two identical $-CH_2CH_3$ groups. Achiral — optically inactive.

B (4-chloropent-2-ene): Reduction gives 2-chloropentane. Cl-bearing carbon has $-H$, $-Cl$, $-CH_3$, and $-CH_2CH_2CH_3$ — four different groups. Chiral centre — optically active.

C (3-chloro-2,4-dimethylpent-1-ene): Reduction gives 3-chloro-2,4-dimethylpentane. Cl-bearing carbon has two identical $-CH(CH_3)_2$ groups. Achiral — optically inactive.

D (4-chlorohept-2-ene): Reduction gives 4-chloroheptane. Cl-bearing carbon has two identical $-CH_2CH_2CH_3$ groups. Achiral — optically inactive.

Only compound B gives an optically active haloalkane.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What volume of $0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$ needs to be added to $100 \mathrm{ml}$ of $0.4 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COONa}^2$ solution to prepare a buffer of pH equal to 4.91 ? ($\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{a}}$ of $\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{COOH}$ is 4.76)
questions.solution:
The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation for an acidic buffer is given by:

$\text{pH} = \text{pK}_{a} + \log \left( \dfrac{[\text{Salt}]}{[\text{Acid}]} \right)$

Given $\text{pH} = 4.91$, $\text{pK}_{a} = 4.76$, and the concentration of salt $[\text{CH}_{3}\text{COONa}] = 0.4 \text{ M}$ with volume $V_{s} = 100 \text{ ml}$.

Substituting the values into the equation:

$4.91 = 4.76 + \log \left( \dfrac{n_{\text{salt}}}{n_{\text{acid}}} \right)$

$0.15 = \log \left( \dfrac{0.4 \times 100}{0.2 \times V_{a}} \right)$

Taking the antilog of both sides:

$10^{0.15} = \dfrac{40}{0.2 \times V_{a}}$

$1.4125 = \dfrac{40}{0.2 \times V_{a}}$

$0.2 \times V_{a} = \dfrac{40}{1.4125}$

$0.2 \times V_{a} = 28.3186$

$V_{a} = \dfrac{28.3186}{0.2} = 141.59 \text{ ml}$

Answer: 141.59 ml

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Solubility product of the sparingly soluble salt $\mathrm{AgBrO}_3$ in aqueous medium is $9.3 \times 10^{-10}$ Calculate the mass in gram of $\mathrm{AgBrO}_3$ present in 100 ml of its saturated solution.
(Molar mass of $\mathrm{AgBrO}_3$ is $236 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ )
questions.solution:
The solubility equilibrium for $\mathrm{AgBrO}_3$ is given by:
$\mathrm{AgBrO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \mathrm{BrO}_3^{-}(aq)$

Let $s$ be the solubility of $\mathrm{AgBrO}_3$ in mol/L. Then $[\mathrm{Ag}^{+}] = s$ and $[\mathrm{BrO}_3^{-}] = s$.

The solubility product constant $K_{sp}$ is defined as:
$K_{sp} = [\mathrm{Ag}^{+}][\mathrm{BrO}_3^{-}] = s^2$

Given $K_{sp} = 9.3 \times 10^{-10}$, we have:
$s = \sqrt{9.3 \times 10^{-10}} = \sqrt{93 \times 10^{-11}} = \sqrt{9.3} \times 10^{-5} \approx 3.04959 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol/L}$

The volume of the solution is $100 \text{ ml} = 0.1 \text{ L}$.

The number of moles of $\mathrm{AgBrO}_3$ in $0.1 \text{ L}$ is:
$n = s \times V = 3.04959 \times 10^{-5} \text{ mol/L} \times 0.1 \text{ L} = 3.04959 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol}$

The molar mass of $\mathrm{AgBrO}_3$ is $236 \text{ g/mol}$. The mass $m$ is:
$m = n \times \text{Molar Mass} = 3.04959 \times 10^{-6} \text{ mol} \times 236 \text{ g/mol}$
$m = 719.705 \times 10^{-6} \text{ g} = 7.19705 \times 10^{-4} \text{ g}$

Answer: $7.197 \times 10^{-4}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Choose the correct statement.
options: Calcium and Magnesium metals are manufactured by electrolysis of aqueous solutions of their salts
The oxo-anion $\mathrm{ClO}_3^{-}$ does not undergo disproportionation reaction
Nitride ion \(\mathrm{N}^{-3}\) cannot act as an oxidising agent
In alkaline medium the reduction of $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}$ ion involves gain of 5 electrons
questions.solution:
Calcium and Magnesium are highly reactive metals with standard reduction potentials more negative than that of water. Electrolysis of their aqueous salt solutions results in the evolution of hydrogen gas at the cathode rather than the deposition of the metal. Therefore, they are manufactured by the electrolysis of their molten chloride salts.

The chlorate ion $\mathrm{ClO}_{3}^{-}$ contains chlorine in the $+5$ oxidation state. It can undergo disproportionation into chloride ($-1$) and perchlorate ($+7$) ions, especially in acidic or basic conditions, making the statement that it does not undergo disproportionation incorrect.

The nitride ion $\mathrm{N}^{3-}$ has nitrogen in its lowest possible oxidation state of $-3$. Since it cannot be reduced further, it cannot act as an oxidizing agent. It can only act as a reducing agent by losing electrons to form nitrogen gas or other nitrogen-containing species.

In an alkaline medium, the reduction of the permanganate ion $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ (where Mn is $+7$) typically proceeds to the manganate ion $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{2-}$ (where Mn is $+6$), which involves a gain of 1 electron, or to manganese dioxide $\mathrm{MnO}_{2}$ (where Mn is $+4$), which involves a gain of 3 electrons. The gain of 5 electrons occurs in an acidic medium where $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$ is reduced to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$.

Answer: Nitride ion \(\mathrm{N}^{-3}\) cannot act as an oxidising agent

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
Which one of the following options represents the decreasing order of oxidation number of the central atom in:
$\mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7^{2-}, \mathrm{CrO}_2^{-}, \mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}, \mathrm{BrO}_3^{-}$
questions.solution:
For $\mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-}$: Let the oxidation number of Cr be $x$. Then $2x + 7(-2) = -2$, which gives $2x = 12$, so $x = +6$.

For $\mathrm{CrO}_{2}^{-}$: Let the oxidation number of Cr be $x$. Then $x + 2(-2) = -1$, which gives $x - 4 = -1$, so $x = +3$.

For $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-}$: Let the oxidation number of Mn be $x$. Then $x + 4(-2) = -1$, which gives $x - 8 = -1$, so $x = +7$.

For $\mathrm{BrO}_{3}^{-}$: Let the oxidation number of Br be $x$. Then $x + 3(-2) = -1$, which gives $x - 6 = -1$, so $x = +5$.

Comparing the oxidation numbers: $\mathrm{MnO}_{4}^{-} (+7) \gt \mathrm{Cr}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{7}^{2-} (+6) \gt \mathrm{BrO}_{3}^{-} (+5) \gt \mathrm{CrO}_{2}^{-} (+3)$.

Answer: $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} \gt \mathrm{Cr}_2 \mathrm{O}_7^{2-} \gt \mathrm{BrO}_3^{-} \gt \mathrm{CrO}_2^{-}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: The concentration and percentage purity of Oxalic acid can be determined by titration with $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ in presence of dil. $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$. Instead of dil. $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4$, dil HCl cannot be used because
options: HCl can also oxidise Oxalic acid to $\mathrm{CO}_2$ and $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$.
HCl can also provide $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions in addition to $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ions from Oxalic acid.
questions.solution:
The titration of oxalic acid with potassium permanganate ($\mathrm{KMnO}_4$) is performed in an acidic medium to ensure the reduction of $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}$ to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$.

The balanced chemical equation for the reaction is: $5\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{C}_2\mathrm{O}_4 + 2\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + 6\mathrm{H}^{+} \rightarrow 10\mathrm{CO}_2 + 2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$.

Dilute sulfuric acid ($\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4$) is used because it is a non-oxidizing acid and provides the necessary $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ ions without interfering with the redox reaction.

If dilute hydrochloric acid ($\mathrm{HCl}$) is used, the chloride ions ($\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$) present in the solution act as a reducing agent. The strong oxidizing agent $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ reacts with $\mathrm{HCl}$ according to the reaction: $2\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-} + 16\mathrm{H}^{+} + 10\mathrm{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 5\mathrm{Cl}_2 + 8\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}$.

Since $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ oxidizes $\mathrm{HCl}$ to chlorine gas ($\mathrm{Cl}_2$), the volume of $\mathrm{KMnO}_4$ consumed will be higher than the stoichiometric amount required for the titration of oxalic acid, leading to inaccurate results. Thus, $\mathrm{HCl}$ is not used because it reduces the permanganate ion.

Answer: $\mathrm{HCl}$ can also reduce $\mathrm{MnO}_4^{-}$ to $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a 1.0 molal solution containing the non-volatile solute Urea, the elevation in boiling point is 2.0 K while the depression in freezing point in a 3.0 molal solution having the same solvent is $4.0 K$. If the ratio $\dfrac{K_b}{K_f}=\dfrac{1}{X}$, what is the value of $X$ ?
questions.solution:
The elevation in boiling point is given by $\Delta T_b = K_b \times m_1$, where $m_1 = 1.0$ molal and $\Delta T_b = 2.0$ K. Thus, $2.0 = K_b \times 1.0$, which implies $K_b = 2.0$ K kg mol$^{-1}$.

The depression in freezing point is given by $\Delta T_f = K_f \times m_2$, where $m_2 = 3.0$ molal and $\Delta T_f = 4.0$ K. Thus, $4.0 = K_f \times 3.0$, which implies $K_f = \dfrac{4.0}{3.0} = \dfrac{4}{3}$ K kg mol$^{-1}$.

The ratio $\dfrac{K_b}{K_f}$ is calculated as $\dfrac{2.0}{4/3} = 2.0 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{6}{4} = \dfrac{3}{2}$.

Given $\dfrac{K_b}{K_f} = \dfrac{1}{X}$, we have $\dfrac{3}{2} = \dfrac{1}{X}$, which implies $X = \dfrac{2}{3}$.

Answer: $\dfrac{2}{3}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A non-volatile solute A weighing 60 g when dissolved in 212 g of the solvent Xylene reduces its vapour pressure to $60 \%$. What is the Molar mass of A in $\mathrm{g} / \mathrm{mol}$ ? [MM of xylene $=106 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$ ]
questions.solution:
According to Raoult's law for a non-volatile solute, the relative lowering of vapour pressure is equal to the mole fraction of the solute:

$\dfrac{P^o - P_s}{P^o} = \dfrac{n_A}{n_A + n_X}$

Given that the vapour pressure is reduced to $60\%$, we have $P_s = 0.6 P^o$. Therefore, $\dfrac{P^o - 0.6 P^o}{P^o} = 0.4$.

The mole fraction of the solute $x_A = \dfrac{n_A}{n_A + n_X} = 0.4$.

This implies $\dfrac{n_X}{n_A} = \dfrac{1 - 0.4}{0.4} = \dfrac{0.6}{0.4} = 1.5$.

The number of moles of solvent Xylene is $n_X = \dfrac{212 \text{ g}}{106 \text{ g/mol}} = 2 \text{ mol}$.

Substituting $n_X$ into the ratio: $\dfrac{2}{n_A} = 1.5 \Rightarrow n_A = \dfrac{2}{1.5} = \dfrac{4}{3} \text{ mol}$.

The molar mass of solute A is $M_A = \dfrac{\text{mass}_A}{n_A} = \dfrac{60 \text{ g}}{4/3 \text{ mol}} = 60 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 45 \text{ g/mol}$.

Answer: $45$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Two volatile liquids X and Y form an ideal solution at 298 K and have vapour pressures equal to 100 mm and 200 mm of Hg respectively in their pure state. The mole fraction of X in the solution is 0.4 and the mole fraction of Y in the vapour phase is a/20. Calculate the value of a.
questions.solution:
Given the pure vapour pressures $P^{\circ}_{X} = 100$ mm Hg and $P^{\circ}_{Y} = 200$ mm Hg.

The mole fraction of X in the liquid phase is $x_{X} = 0.4$. Therefore, the mole fraction of Y in the liquid phase is $x_{Y} = 1 - 0.4 = 0.6$.

Using Raoult's Law, the partial pressures of X and Y are:
$P_{X} = x_{X} P^{\circ}_{X} = 0.4 \times 100 = 40$ mm Hg
$P_{Y} = x_{Y} P^{\circ}_{Y} = 0.6 \times 200 = 120$ mm Hg

The total pressure of the solution is $P_{total} = P_{X} + P_{Y} = 40 + 120 = 160$ mm Hg.

The mole fraction of Y in the vapour phase, denoted as $y_{Y}$, is given by:
$y_{Y} = \dfrac{P_{Y}}{P_{total}} = \dfrac{120}{160} = \dfrac{12}{16} = \dfrac{3}{4} = 0.75$.

Given that $y_{Y} = \dfrac{a}{20}$, we equate the values:
$\dfrac{a}{20} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

$a = \dfrac{3}{4} \times 20 = 3 \times 5 = 15$.

Answer: $15$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: When $9.2 \times 10^{-3} \mathrm{~kg}$ of formic acid is added to 600 ml of water the freezing point of water is depressed. If $30 \%$ of Formic acid undergoes dissociation what would be the freezing point of the solution? ( $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{f}}$ of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$ is $1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol} ; \mathrm{MM}$ of formic acid: 46 amu )
questions.solution:
The molar mass of formic acid (HCOOH) is $46 \text{ g/mol}$. The mass of formic acid is $9.2 \times 10^{-3} \text{ kg} = 9.2 \text{ g}$.

The number of moles of formic acid is $n = \dfrac{9.2}{46} = 0.2 \text{ mol}$.

The mass of water is $600 \text{ ml} = 0.6 \text{ kg}$. The molality $m$ is $\dfrac{0.2}{0.6} = \dfrac{1}{3} \text{ mol/kg}$.

Formic acid dissociates as $\text{HCOOH} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}^{+} + \text{HCOO}^{-}$. For $30\%$ dissociation, the degree of dissociation $\alpha = 0.3$.

The van't Hoff factor $i = 1 + \alpha(n-1)$, where $n=2$. Thus, $i = 1 + 0.3(2-1) = 1.3$.

The depression in freezing point is $\Delta T_f = i \times K_f \times m = 1.3 \times 1.86 \times \dfrac{1}{3} = 1.3 \times 0.62 = 0.806 \text{ K}$.

The freezing point of the solution is $T_f = T_f^{\circ} - \Delta T_f = 273.15 - 0.806 = 272.344 \text{ K}$.

Answer: 272.3 K

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Choose the correct statement.
options: For a solvent, $\quad K_b=\dfrac{R \times M_1 \times T_b^2}{1000 \times \Delta \text { Hvap }}\left(\mathrm{R}=\right.$ Gas constant, $M_1=$ Molar mass of solvent, $T_b=B . P$ of the solvent $)$
Hypotonic solution is more concentrated with respect to the other solution separated by a semi permeable membrane
A 1.0 molal solution of Glucose in water is more concentrated than 1.0 M glucose solution in the same solvent.
A solution formed by adding Carbon di-sulphide to Acetone forms a maximum boiling azeotrope.
questions.solution:
(1) Correct: $K_b = \dfrac{R \times M_1 \times T_b^2}{1000 \times \Delta H_{vap}}$ is the standard thermodynamic expression for the ebullioscopic constant, where $R$ is the gas constant, $M_1$ is the molar mass of solvent, $T_b$ is the boiling point of pure solvent, and $\Delta H_{vap}$ is the molar enthalpy of vaporization.

(2) Incorrect: A hypotonic solution has lower solute concentration. The solution with higher concentration is called hypertonic.

(3) Incorrect: 1.0 M solution has 1 mole of glucose in 1 L of solution (less than 1 kg of solvent), while 1.0 m solution has 1 mole in exactly 1 kg of solvent. Hence 1.0 M is more concentrated than 1.0 m, not less.

(4) Incorrect: $CS_2$ + Acetone shows positive deviation from Raoult's law (weaker A-B interactions), forming a minimum boiling azeotrope, not a maximum boiling azeotrope.

The correct statement is (1).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
If X is a haloalkane with a single Chlorine atom per molecule and the percentage of Cl is 55 , what would be the number of Cl atoms present in 0.1 g of the haloalkane?
Atomic mass of $\mathrm{Cl}=35.5 \mathrm{~g} / \mathrm{mol}$
questions.solution:
Let the molar mass of the haloalkane be $M$ g/mol. The percentage of Chlorine is given as $55\%$.

Since there is one Chlorine atom per molecule, the mass of Chlorine in one mole of the haloalkane is $35.5$ g. Therefore, $\dfrac{35.5}{M} \times 100 = 55$.

$M = \dfrac{35.5 \times 100}{55} = \dfrac{3550}{55} \approx 64.545$ g/mol.

The number of moles of the haloalkane in $0.1$ g is $n = \dfrac{0.1}{64.545} \approx 0.001549$ moles.

Since each molecule contains one Chlorine atom, the number of moles of Chlorine atoms is equal to the number of moles of the haloalkane, which is $0.001549$ moles.

The number of Chlorine atoms is $N = n \times N_{A} = 0.001549 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} \approx 9.328 \times 10^{20}$.

Answer: $9.328 \times 10^{20}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A certain orbital having 2 angular nodes and no radial nodes is:
questions.solution:
The number of angular nodes in an orbital is given by the azimuthal quantum number $l$.

The number of radial nodes in an orbital is given by the formula $n - l - 1$, where $n$ is the principal quantum number.

Given that the orbital has 2 angular nodes, we have $l = 2$. This corresponds to a d-orbital.

Given that the orbital has 0 radial nodes, we have $n - l - 1 = 0$.

Substituting $l = 2$ into the radial node equation: $n - 2 - 1 = 0 \Rightarrow n = 3$.

Therefore, the orbital is $3d$.

Answer: 3 d

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A certain gas absorbs photon of wavelength $4.0 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$ and emits radiation at two wavelengths. If one of the emissions occurs at $7.5 \times 10^{-7} \mathrm{~m}$, what is the wavelength at which the second emission occurs?
questions.solution:
The energy of the absorbed photon is given by $E_{abs} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{abs}}$.

The energy of the emitted photons are $E_{1} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{1}}$ and $E_{2} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}$.

According to the principle of conservation of energy, the energy absorbed must equal the sum of the energies emitted in the two-step process: $E_{abs} = E_{1} + E_{2}$.

Substituting the expressions for energy: $\dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{abs}} = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{1}} + \dfrac{hc}{\lambda_{2}}$.

Dividing by $hc$: $\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{abs}} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{1}} + \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{2}}$.

Given $\lambda_{abs} = 4.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 400 \text{ nm}$ and $\lambda_{1} = 7.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = 750 \text{ nm}$.

$\dfrac{1}{400} = \dfrac{1}{750} + \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{2}}$.

$\dfrac{1}{\lambda_{2}} = \dfrac{1}{400} - \dfrac{1}{750} = \dfrac{750 - 400}{400 \times 750} = \dfrac{350}{300000} = \dfrac{35}{30000} = \dfrac{7}{6000}$.

$\lambda_{2} = \dfrac{6000}{7} \approx 857.14 \text{ nm}$.

Answer: 857 nm

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Given that the standard enthalpy of combustion of $\mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{S})}$ and $\mathrm{CS}_2(\mathrm{l})$ are -393.3 and $-1108.76 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$ respectively and the standard enthalpy of formation of $\mathrm{CS}_2$ is $128.02 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$. What is $\Delta H_f^0$ of $\mathrm{SO}_2$ ?
questions.solution:
The combustion reactions are given as follows:

1. $\mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{s})} + \mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})}$, $\Delta H_1 = -393.3 \text{ kJ/mol}$

2. $\mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})} + 3\mathrm{O}_{2(\mathrm{g})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CO}_{2(\mathrm{g})} + 2\mathrm{SO}_{2(\mathrm{g})}$, $\Delta H_2 = -1108.76 \text{ kJ/mol}$

The enthalpy of formation of $\mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})}$ is given by the reaction:

3. $\mathrm{C}_{(\mathrm{s})} + 2\mathrm{S}_{(\mathrm{s})} \rightarrow \mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})}$, $\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CS}_2) = 128.02 \text{ kJ/mol}$

The enthalpy of combustion of $\mathrm{CS}_{2(\mathrm{l})}$ can be expressed in terms of enthalpies of formation:

$\Delta H_2 = [\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO}_2) + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2)] - [\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CS}_2) + 3\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{O}_2)]$

Since $\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{CO}_2) = \Delta H_1 = -393.3 \text{ kJ/mol}$ and $\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{O}_2) = 0$, we substitute the values:

$-1108.76 = [-393.3 + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2)] - [128.02 + 0]$

$-1108.76 = -393.3 + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2) - 128.02$

$-1108.76 = -521.32 + 2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2)$

$2\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2) = -1108.76 + 521.32 = -587.44$

$\Delta H_f^0(\mathrm{SO}_2) = -293.72 \text{ kJ/mol}$

Answer: $-293.72 \mathrm{~kJ} / \mathrm{mol}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
0.4 g of Propane burns completely at 300 K in a bomb calorimeter. The temperature of the calorimeter and surrounding water rises by $0.4^0 \mathrm{C}$.
If the heat capacity of the calorimeter and contents is $24 \mathrm{~kJ} \mathrm{~K}^{-1}$ what is the Enthalpy for the reaction?
(Assume that propane gas shows ideal behaviour).
questions.solution:
The combustion reaction of propane is given by: $C_{3}H_{8}(g) + 5O_{2}(g) \rightarrow 3CO_{2}(g) + 4H_{2}O(l)$.

The heat released in the bomb calorimeter is $q_{v} = C \times \Delta T$, where $C = 24 \text{ kJ K}^{-1}$ and $\Delta T = 0.4 \text{ K}$.

$q_{v} = 24 \times 0.4 = 9.6 \text{ kJ}$.

The number of moles of propane ($C_{3}H_{8}$) is $n = \dfrac{0.4 \text{ g}}{44 \text{ g mol}^{-1}} = \dfrac{0.4}{44} \text{ mol} = \dfrac{1}{110} \text{ mol}$.

The internal energy change for the combustion of 1 mole of propane is $\Delta U = -\dfrac{q_{v}}{n} = -9.6 \times 110 = -1056 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$.
